adults.title: When Someone You Love Has Stepped Away
adults.big_idea: We cannot change the hearts of loved ones who have turned from the Lord, but Jesus Christ can, so we hand Him our despair and keep loving them the way He does.
adults.objective: Learners will name one burden of worry or guilt for a loved one that they will turn over to Jesus Christ, and choose one way to show that person love this week.
prepare: Read Elder Rasband's talk, especially paragraphs T18.03, T18.08, T18.12 and the three suggestions (T18.23–T18.25).
Bring a slip of paper and a pen or pencil for each person.
Write on the board: Love is not ... / Love is ...
Pray by name for class members who carry this ache. Decide beforehand that no one will be asked to share names or family details.

segments.name: A name in your heart
steps: Begin with prayer. Explain that Elder Rasband said his message was for everyone whose heart aches for loved ones who have turned away from the Lord, and that he and Sister Rasband have felt that anguish too.
Hand out the slips of paper. Invite each person to write, silently and privately, the first name or initials of someone they love and worry about. Tell them no one will see the paper.
Say that today is not about fixing that person. It is about what the Savior offers to the one holding the paper.
Sing or read the words of the song Elder Rasband quoted from, Love One Another, if time allows.

segments.name: What we have tried
steps: Read paragraph T18.03 aloud, slowly. Elder Rasband lists what we do in our grief: preach, cajole, argue, demand, lecture, ignore, even send links to conference talks.
Invite pairs to talk for two minutes about the first question below. Remind them to speak about their own feelings, not about the other person's choices.
Bring the class back and read the one-sentence paragraph T18.04. Ask the second question and take two or three responses.
questions: Without naming anyone, which of the things on Elder Rasband's list do you recognize in yourself, and what did it do to the relationship?
Why do you think Heavenly Father designed His plan so that everyone must choose for themselves to follow Jesus Christ?

segments.name: Whose battle is it?
steps: Ask everyone to turn to 2 Chronicles 20:15 and read it silently, looking for whose battle it is. Elder Rasband called this verse the answer.
Have a class member read the first key quote and the invitation from paragraph T18.08 aloud. Point out that the speaker asked us to listen carefully before he gave it.
Discuss the questions below. Let silence do its work; these questions deserve time.
Read President Oaks's words from the aligned quotes: the Lord is still pursuing the person on their slip of paper.
Give one quiet minute. Invite learners to write under the name on their paper one specific worry, regret or what-if they want to turn over to the Savior.
questions: What is the difference between turning our despair over to Jesus Christ and giving up on someone?
Elder Rasband taught that our loved ones are foremost children of our Father in Heaven, who loves them even more than we do. How does that change the way you carry this?
When have you felt the Savior carry a burden for someone you love that you could not carry?

segments.name: What love is, and is not
steps: Divide into groups of three or four. Ask each group to read paragraph T18.12 and Luke 15:20 together and fill in the two columns on the board: what love is not, and what love is.
Invite a spokesperson from each group to add one line to the board. Notice together that love does not mean stepping back, and it does not mean approving of every decision.
Read President Monson's sentence from the aligned quotes. Ask the first question below.

Briefly recall Alma the Younger as Elder Rasband told it: his father prayed with much faith, an angel said those prayers were heard, and the young man remembered his father's teaching about Jesus Christ and was filled with joy. Ask the second question.
questions: Think of your next conversation with the person on your paper. What would it look like to put the person ahead of the problem?
Elder Rasband said the prodigal son came back because of love, and that he knew where to find it. What helps a person know that our home and our hearts are a place to come back to?

segments.name: Three suggestions for finding rest
steps: Write Elder Rasband's three suggestions on the board in a few words each: let go of guilt and never give up; love the person more than the problem; remember Jesus Christ is the answer, seek Him and pray mightily.
Ask learners to read Matthew 11:28–29 silently and mark what the Savior asks of us and what He promises.
Invite each person to choose the one suggestion they most need and write on the back of their paper one thing they will do about it before next Sunday.
Check for understanding: ask two or three volunteers to finish this sentence in their own words, without names: This week, loving like Jesus will mean that I ...
questions: Which of the three suggestions is hardest for you right now, and why?

segments.name: An apostle's promise
steps: Read Elder Rasband's promise in paragraph T18.26: when the storm pulls loved ones off course, it will have no power to drag us down if the rock we are built on is Jesus Christ.
Bear your own brief testimony that the Savior knows and loves the people on those slips of paper.

Invite learners to keep the paper in their scriptures and to pray by name for that person each day. Tell them you will begin next week by asking what they noticed as they turned their worry over to the Lord.

key_quotes.text: We cannot change their hearts, but He can; He is a God of miracles.

Love is not stepping back or sanctioning others’ decisions and actions. Love is being interested in their lives, their successes, and their challenges. Love is being there with arms outstretched and a cheerful countenance.
We fail only when we give up and stop trying, so never, never give up on those you love.
By the power of Jesus Christ’s Atonement, there is always a way back!

scriptures.use: Read silently at the start of the third segment; look for whose battle it is, then connect it to the invitation to turn our despair over to Jesus Christ.
Read in small groups with paragraph T18.12; list what the father did when he saw his son and add it to the Love is column on the board.
Read silently in the fifth segment; mark what the Savior asks of us and what He promises to those who are heavy laden.
Optional for a longer class: read aloud and ask what this verse teaches a parent, friend or leader who has prayed for a long time.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Thomas S. Monson
aligned_quotes.text: Never let a problem to be solved become more important than a person to be loved.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: He is relentless in His loving pursuit of each of you.

invitations.text: I ask you to turn over to Jesus Christ your despair for those wayward souls.

takeaways: I cannot change another person's heart, but Jesus Christ can.
Love is neither stepping back nor approving every choice; it is staying interested, staying near and staying hopeful.
I fail only if I give up, so I will keep loving and keep praying.
act: Each day this week, pray by name for the person on your paper, and in that prayer tell Heavenly Father the specific worry you are handing to the Savior.
Reach out once to that person with no agenda at all: ask about something that matters to them and simply listen.
The next time guilt or a what-if keeps you awake, read Matthew 11:28–29 and say aloud that you trust the Savior with this.
Before a hard conversation, pause and ask yourself whether you are about to put the problem ahead of the person.
adapt: At home with a spouse or a few adults: skip the groups, read paragraphs T18.08 and T18.12 together, and end by kneeling to pray by name for the person you are both thinking of.
Large class: do every discussion in pairs or threes first, then take only two comments from the whole room so everyone talks and you still finish.
Only 15 minutes: do the slip of paper, the third segment on 2 Chronicles 20:15 and paragraph T18.08, and the promise at the end.

youth.title: You Can't Change a Heart. He Can.
youth.big_idea: When someone we care about steps away from the Savior, our part is to love them and pray for them, and Jesus Christ's part is to change hearts and bring them home.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain the difference between pushing someone and loving someone like Jesus, and will choose one person to pray for by name and reach out to this week.
prepare: Read Elder Rasband's talk, especially paragraphs T18.03, T18.08, T18.12 and T18.14–T18.21.
Bring paper and pens, and a timer (a phone works).
Write on the board: My part / His part.
Ask youth to bring scriptures, paper or on their phones.

segments.name: Sixty-second list
steps: Start right after the prayer. Split into two or three teams and give each a sheet of paper.
Set a timer for sixty seconds. Teams write every way people try to get someone else to change, whether it works or not.

Read paragraph T18.03 aloud. Teams score a point for every item on their list that matches Elder Rasband's: preach, cajole, argue, demand, lecture, ignore, sit them down to watch general conference, send links to talks.

Ask the question below, then say that Elder Rasband spoke to everyone whose heart aches for a loved one who has turned away from the Lord. Many youth know that feeling about a friend, a brother or sister, or someone else they love.
questions: Elder Rasband said these efforts can cause a greater rift. Why do you think pushing so often backfires?

segments.name: My part, His part
steps: Have one youth read paragraph T18.04 and another read the second key quote from T18.08.

As a class, sort ideas into the two columns on the board. Under His part: change hearts, heal, pay for sins, bring them home. Under My part, leave space; you will fill it in during the next two segments.
Read Elder Rasband's invitation from T18.08, and his short summary of what the Savior says to all who grieve: “I’ve got this!”
Discuss the questions below honestly. It is fine if some answers are I don't know yet.
questions: Is it a relief or is it frustrating that you cannot make someone else believe? Why?
What do you think it actually looks like to turn your worry about someone over to Jesus Christ?

segments.name: Two stories, two groups
steps: Divide the class in two. Group one reads Mosiah 27:14 and Alma 36:17–20 with paragraphs T18.14–T18.15. Group two reads Luke 15:11–24 with paragraphs T18.19–T18.21.
Each group has four minutes to find two things: what the person who loved did, and what the Lord did. They choose a reporter.

Each reporter has one minute to retell the story and give the two answers. Add what the loving person did to the My part column: prayed with much faith, kept watching, ran to meet him, had compassion.
Point out a detail from each story as Elder Rasband told it: young Alma remembered what his father had taught him about Jesus Christ, and the prodigal son knew where to find love.
questions: Elder Rasband said Alma's father may have prayed for years, maybe decades. What keeps a person praying that long?
What does it take to be the kind of friend or family member someone knows they can come back to?

segments.name: Love is not, love is
steps: Ask everyone to read paragraph T18.12 on their phones or from your copy and find what love is not and what love is.

Raise the honest question many youth ask: if I stay close to a friend who has stopped believing, does that mean I agree with everything they do? Let them answer from T18.12, then read Elder Gilbert's sentence from the aligned quotes.

Role play in pairs for two minutes. One person is a friend who says they are done with church. The other responds using only what T18.12 describes: interest in their life, a cheerful face, no lecture. Then switch.
Ask two pairs what was hard about it and what felt right.
questions: What is one sentence you could say to a friend that shows you care about them and not only about their choices?

segments.name: One person, one week
steps: Give everyone a minute of silence to think of one person they care about who is drifting or struggling. They write the initials where only they will see them.

Invite them to take out their phones and draft, but not yet send, a short message to that person that is only about that person's life: a question, a memory, a good luck for something coming up. No links, no sermon.
Challenge them to pray for that person by name every day for seven days and to send the message or say it in person when it feels right.
Check for understanding: ask a volunteer to explain the two columns on the board to the class in fifteen seconds.

segments.name: Built on the rock
steps: Read Helaman 5:12 together, then tell them Elder Rasband used this verse to make a promise as an Apostle: the storm that pulls loved ones off course will have no power to drag us down if we are built on Jesus Christ.
Read the last key quote from T18.18 and bear a short testimony that the Savior knows and loves the person each of them is thinking of.
Tell them you will ask next week, without names, how the seven days of prayer went and what they noticed.

key_quotes.text: By divine design, brothers and sisters, everyone must choose for themselves to follow Jesus Christ.
We cannot change their hearts, but He can; He is a God of miracles.
Love is being interested in their lives, their successes, and their challenges.
He gave His very life to bring them home, all the way home.

scriptures.use: Group one reads it and finds what the angel said about why he came; connect it to a father's prayers of faith.
Group one reads it and finds what Alma remembered, what he cried in his heart, and what he felt afterward.
Group two reads the parable and lists what the father did when he saw his son a great way off.
Read together in the last segment; ask what the rock is and what the verse promises about the storm.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Gilbert
aligned_quotes.text: For disciples of Jesus Christ, truth and love always walk together.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Thomas S. Monson
aligned_quotes.text: Never let a problem to be solved become more important than a person to be loved.

invitations.text: I ask you to turn over to Jesus Christ your despair for those wayward souls.

takeaways: Everyone has to choose for themselves to follow Jesus Christ; I cannot choose for them.
My part is to love, stay interested and pray. Changing hearts is the Savior's part.
If I am built on Jesus Christ, someone else's storm will not drag me down.
act: Pray by name for one person every day for seven days.
Send or say one message this week that is only about that person's life, with no lecture attached.
When you feel like arguing or giving up on someone, stop and say a short prayer handing that worry to the Savior.
Read Alma 36:17–20 once this week and notice what brought Alma back.
adapt: At home with one or two youth: skip the teams, read the two stories together, and let each person share which one they relate to more.
Small class: do the two stories as one group, giving half the time to each.
Short on time: do the sixty-second list, the My part and His part columns, and the one person, one week challenge.

children.title: Arms Open Wide
children.big_idea: Jesus loves everyone, and I can love others like Jesus does.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Jesus loves everyone and show one way they will love someone this week.
prepare: Read paragraphs T18.11–T18.14 and T18.19–T18.21 of Elder Rasband's talk and Luke 15:20.
Bring a flashlight, a soft ball, paper and crayons.
Clear a little space so children can walk from one side of the room to the other.
Be ready to sing Love One Another.

segments.name: Sing and begin
steps: Invite a child to pray.
Sing Love One Another together. Tell the children that Elder Rasband, an Apostle, quoted this song in general conference.
Teach today's truth with actions: Jesus loves everyone (arms open wide), and I can love like Jesus (hands on heart). Say it together three times.

segments.name: The father who ran
steps: Tell the story Jesus told, in simple words: a son went far away from home. After a while he was sad and wanted to come back. While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, felt love for him, and ran to him.

Act it out. Choose one child to be the father on one side of the room. The other children walk slowly to the far side, then turn and walk back. The father watches, then hurries to meet them with arms open wide.
Do it again with a new father so more children have a turn.
Explain that Elder Rasband taught that love is what brought the son home, and that Heavenly Father holds out His arms to all His children.
questions: How do you think the son felt when he saw his father running to him?
How does it feel when someone is happy to see you?

segments.name: Light that reaches everyone
steps: Dim the lights if you can. Turn on the flashlight and shine it on the floor near you. Invite a child to stand close, in the light.
Ask another child to stand far across the room. Ask the class if the light can reach that far. Shine it all the way to that child.
Let two or three children take a turn holding the flashlight and shining it gently on the floor by a friend who is far away.
Say that the love of Jesus is like this light. It reaches people who are near and people who are far. Repeat today's truth with the actions.
questions: Is there anyone the love of Jesus cannot reach?

segments.name: What love looks like
steps: Read the second key quote slowly and show what a cheerful countenance is: a happy, friendly face. Have everyone show you theirs.
Tell the children that Elder Rasband taught we become more like the Savior when we are peacemakers and when we are patient, forgiving and kind.

Sit in a circle and roll or gently toss the ball. Whoever catches it names one kind thing they can do or say, then passes it on. Help younger children with ideas: share, say sorry, sit by someone, smile, help.
Play a quick round of show me: name a simple situation, such as a friend drops their crayons or someone new comes to class, and let the children show with their bodies what love would do.
questions: What is one way someone showed love to you this week?

segments.name: Love prays
steps: Read the third key quote. Explain that one way we love people is to pray for them.
Tell the children that in the Book of Mormon a father named Alma prayed with much faith for his son, and Heavenly Father heard his prayers.
Invite the children to fold their arms, close their eyes, and think of one person they love. Give them a quiet moment to think about what they could ask Heavenly Father to bless that person with.
Ask one or two children to share the kind of thing they might pray for, such as help to feel happy or help at school.

segments.name: Draw your open arms
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Invite them to draw themselves with arms open wide, and next to them a person they will show love to this week.
As they draw, move around the room and ask each child what they will do for that person. Write their words on the paper for them if they need help.
This is your check for understanding: each child should be able to tell you one thing they will do.

segments.name: Say it once more
steps: Have the children hold up their drawings and say today's truth one more time with the actions.
Say Elder Fale's words from this conference together (see the aligned quote). Bear a short testimony that Jesus Christ loves each of them and everyone they love.
Ask them to take the drawing home and do what they drew. Tell them you will ask next week what they did.
Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: Jesus Christ is the perfect embodiment of love.
Love is being there with arms outstretched and a cheerful countenance.

scriptures.use: Open the Bible to this verse as you tell the story so the children see where it comes from; an older child can read it aloud before you act it out.
After singing Love One Another, show the children this verse and tell them the song comes from what Jesus asked us to do.
Show the verse during the prayer segment and explain in your own words that Heavenly Father heard a father's prayers for his son.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: Jesus loves everyone, near and far.
I can love like Jesus with kind words, open arms and a happy face.
I can pray for the people I love.
act: Do the kind thing you drew for the person in your picture.
Say a prayer this week for someone you love and use their name.
Greet someone with a smile and open arms when they come home or come to class.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7, keep each part short and moving. Act out the father running two or three times, repeat the truth with actions after every activity, and roll the ball instead of tossing it. Let a helper sit with the youngest during drawing and write their words. Shorten the prayer segment to one quiet moment with folded arms.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11, have a child read Luke 15:20 and John 15:12 aloud and let an older child lead the ball game or the flashlight activity. Ask a harder question: Elder Rasband taught that love is being interested in other people's lives; what is the difference between being kind to someone and really being interested in them? Invite them to write, not only draw, their plan.
